title: MuEdit: An efficient multi-task editing method towards inter-domain knowledge conflicts
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Prior methods conflict when editing tasks sequentially and degrade; ours projects into a common null space, avoiding conflict and preserving performance.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; left contrast diagram with t-SNE plots, right radial bar chart
description: Two-part figure. Panel (a) on a cream background contrasts 'Traditional Methods' (red title) with 'Mu-Edit' (green title) in two columns. Each column shows a flow diagram: Task C's Δ is projected to PΔ, with W_A and W_B nodes and Task A/B network icons below. The traditional side loops back with a red 'Conflict!' label, while Mu-Edit shows a 'Common Null Space of A and B' and a green 'No Conflict!' label. Below, two t-SNE scatter plots show null-space hidden representations: the traditional one has separated, interlocking blue and red clusters, and Mu-Edit's has overlapping blue and green clusters. Panel (b) is a circular radial bar chart titled 'Multi-task editing performance decline'. It has striped (before) and solid (after) bars colored by task (Spec, Gen, Loc, Safe, SQuAD, SST-2) and grouped by method (FT, ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit), with legends at the right and bottom.
caption: Mechanism and motivation of our Mu-Edit, specifically: (a) Visualization of Mu-Edit's null space projection mechanism. (b) Empirical validation results of existing methods' performance decline after editing sequentially across different tasks.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.
